source.title: Scaling Laws For Scalable Oversight
source.authors: Joshua Engels; David D. Baek; Subhash Kantamneni; Max Tegmark

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as related work but studies oversight-game performance against general Elo, not held-out pretraining loss or the parameter/token/compute scaling claims.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, sweep parameter count, training tokens or compute, test small-run extrapolations, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its own results concern oversight-game domain Elo as a function of Chatbot Arena Elo. Those related findings are recorded under fits_no_version; they do not test the listed claim versions. The text also reports prompt-based, game-specific results that are not evidence about ordinary pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study regresses game-specific Domain Elo on Chatbot Arena Elo for 13–14 proprietary and open models. It never varies parameters, tokens or compute and never measures pretraining loss. Its x-axis is a capability proxy, not scale or pretraining loss, so it does not bear on V6 either. Kaplan et al. appears only in related work, as a contrast ('In contrast to this literature').
record.authors_conclusion: Partly wrong. The authors conclude three things. Oversight-game Domain Elo scales with general (Arena) Elo with game-specific slopes. Practitioners should fit these curves, extrapolate them, and iterate designs until the Guard slope exceeds the Houdini slope. Their NSO theory gives success rates at a 400 Elo gap of 13.5% for Mafia, 51.7% for Debate, 10.0% for Backdoor Code and 9.4% for Wargames. The authors do not say their work fails to establish pretraining-loss scaling laws; that framing is the reader's.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops an oversight-game and Elo-fitting framework; it does not reproduce the original language-model pretraining scaling-law methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported relationships differ by game, player role and debate dataset. The paper uses Chatbot Arena Elo as a proxy for general intelligence and selects linear or saturated domain-Elo fits using AIC.

fits_no_version.finding: Guard and Houdini Domain Elo in Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code and Wargames relate roughly linearly to Chatbot Arena Elo. Slopes vary strongly by game and role: Debate Houdini is flat, Backdoor Code Guard is nearly flat, Wargames Houdini is flat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oversight-game performance relates to general capability (Arena Elo) in game- and role-specific ways, approximated by a piecewise-linear Double ReLU.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher-Elo models write more viable backdoors, but given a viable backdoor they are no more likely to evade the Guard.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: General capability raises backdoor validity but not backdoor deceptiveness.

record.problems: The paper says Chatbot Arena Elo is an imperfect proxy for general intelligence; it studies simplified game settings, and its Wargames measure roleplaying rather than actual escape. It notes that the Mafia configuration is limited and that the debate setup assumes faithful adversarial participation. The text gives qualitative descriptions for several plotted trends without numerical curve values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. The theoretical NSO calculations and win-rate estimates concern the paper's oversight framework, not the listed pretraining-loss versions.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Extrapolation of loss from small to large runs: not tested.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count: not tested.
Other modalities or training regimes: not tested.
Downstream performance vs model scale or pretraining loss. The paper uses Chatbot Arena Elo as the predictor and never reports parameters or loss.
Dependence of loss exponents or allocations on fitting choices: not tested. The paper's AIC model selection concerns Elo-vs-Elo fits only.

record.verdict_notes: The title uses 'scaling laws' in a loose sense: the fits are of capability vs capability, not of scale. No row bears on any version. The record's T6 and discusses labels are correct, though cites_only would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss; the paper instead relates game-specific performance to general Elo.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: LLMs in Counting-to-21 (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared game-specific Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Domain Elo as a function of General Elo
rows.value: The text describes a low-end plateau, a linear improvement region, and saturation at higher general Elo.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the tested models; the paper notes deviations at lower general-Elo levels.
rows.check: Counting-to-21 Domain Elo vs Arena Elo is not loss vs scale. The 'observed' state refers to the paper's own Double ReLU hypothesis, not to any claim version.

rows.subject: LLMs in Mafia (aggregate Guard curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Guard Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Guard Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text describes an approximately linear increase; the Guard slope is steeper than the Houdini slope.
rows.note: Aggregate fitted curve across models; the paper reports only one Mafia configuration.

rows.subject: LLMs in Mafia (aggregate Houdini curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Houdini Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Houdini Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text describes an approximately linear increase, with a shallower slope than the Guard curve.

rows.subject: LLMs in Debate (aggregate Guard curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared judge Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Judge Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text says Guard performance scales with general Elo.
rows.note: Aggregate result across models; numerical curve values are not stated in the text.

rows.subject: LLMs in Debate (aggregate Houdini curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared debater Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Debater Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text says Houdini performance stays constant.

rows.subject: LLMs in Debate (aggregate Guard and Houdini results)
rows.operation_detail: Compared judge and debater Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo across datasets.
rows.measure: Guard and Houdini Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text reports similar scaling behavior: judge Domain Elo scales with general Elo, while debater Domain Elo does not.
rows.note: The statement summarizes trends across the datasets; separate numeric results are not stated.

rows.subject: LLMs in Debate (aggregate Guard and Houdini results)
rows.operation_detail: Compared judge and debater Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Guard and Houdini Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text says performance is mostly flat for both Guards and Houdinis.

rows.subject: LLMs in Backdoor Code (aggregate Guard curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Guard Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Guard Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text says Guard Elo scales with general Elo, but its slope is nearly flat.
rows.check: The 'partial' state is judged against the paper's own slope comparison, not against any version. It is an oversight-game measure.

rows.subject: LLMs in Backdoor Code (aggregate Houdini curve)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Houdini Domain Elo with Chatbot Arena general Elo.
rows.measure: Houdini Domain Elo versus General Elo
rows.value: The text says Houdini Elo scales with general Elo and has a steeper slope than the Guard curve.
rows.note: The authors say the higher-intelligence Houdinis are more likely to produce functionally valid backdoors, not more deceptive ones.

rows.subject: LLMs generating viable Backdoor Code backdoors (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured viable-backdoor generation across models with different general Elo.

conditions.value: Backdoor passes the first two success criteria

rows.value: The text says more generally intelligent models generate a greater number of viable backdoors.
rows.note: The plotted result is summarized qualitatively in the text.
rows.check: Viable-backdoor count by model, ordered by Arena Elo. This is not a scale or loss measure.

rows.subject: LLMs generating viable Backdoor Code backdoors (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Guard evasion among viable backdoors written by models with different general Elo.

conditions.value: Conditional on a backdoor being viable

rows.value: The text says more intelligent Houdinis' viable backdoors are no more likely to evade Guard detection.
rows.note: This is a conditional result about deception, distinct from the rate of generating viable backdoors.
